Comparative advantage refers to the ability of a country or individual to produce a particular good or service relative to the production of the same good or service by another country or individual. It is based on the opportunity cost of producing each good or service. The country or individual with a comparative advantage in producing a good or service is able to produce more of that good or service with less input than the country or individual with a comparative disadvantage in producing that good or service. The theory of comparative advantage was developed by David Ricardo, who introduced it in his work "On the Theory of Moral Sentiments" in 1817. The theory of comparative advantage is still widely used in economics and business to explain why countries or individuals are able to produce a particular good or service more efficiently than others.
